headline: High risk of data leakage and capability conflict: Plandex can read/write local project files and use broad egress, while EMQX exposes HTTP APIs and broad egress with IoT data exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: No direct shared channel is documented, but Plandex reads/writes project files and EMQX exposes HTTP APIs, so a manual file or API bridge could carry injected instructions. The pair lacks evidence of default ingestion of each other’s outputs, so this stays low rather than medium.
conditions: IF EMQX output is copied into a Plandex project file or stdin/stdout workflow
IF Plandex is configured to ingest files produced by EMQX or another bridge
mitigations: Keep the agents in separate directories
Disable any manual copy-paste bridge between outputs and prompts
Review imported files before Plandex consumes them
Use a provenance tag or prefix for any bridged content
requires-engineering: add content provenance filtering between the agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: EMQX touches IoT data and has broad network egress; Plandex reads project files and can send context to a model provider or Plandex Cloud/self-hosted server. A shared workspace or copied artifacts could leak sensitive IoT data through Plandex’s outbound calls, so the pathway exists in default-like use.
conditions: IF IoT data from EMQX is placed into Plandex project files
IF Plandex forwards those files or derived context to a model provider or Plandex Cloud
mitigations: Store IoT data outside the Plandex workspace
Redact sensitive fields before importing into Plandex
Use a self-hosted model endpoint with strict retention settings
Restrict EMQX egress to approved destinations
requires-engineering: enforce workspace-level data loss prevention

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Plandex can write the filesystem, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses; EMQX exposes HTTP APIs and broad egress. If both operate on the same project or deployment artifacts, they can race on shared mutable state even though EMQX’s write surface is not documented. Uncertainty about EMQX’s mutability pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF both agents target the same repository or deployment directory
IF EMQX API-driven changes and Plandex file edits occur without locking
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Pause one agent before the other applies changes
Use git locks or a single-writer policy
Review diffs before apply
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level mutual exclusion

D_cascading_error.rationale: Plandex’s review-then-apply flow can still act on upstream content, and EMQX can emit operational data over HTTP APIs. If EMQX output is treated as authoritative input to Plandex, errors can cascade into generated code or commits. The sandbox reduces but does not eliminate this risk.
conditions: IF EMQX output is fed into Plandex without human verification
IF Plandex auto-apply is enabled on plans derived from EMQX data
mitigations: Require human review before apply
Validate EMQX-derived facts against a second source
Disable auto-apply
Keep EMQX telemetry out of plan inputs
requires-engineering: add schema validation for upstream outputs

E_compliance.rationale: EMQX touches IoT data, while Plandex handles source code and may send content to a model provider or Plandex Cloud. If regulated IoT data is mixed into code workflows, retention and residency obligations can diverge. Only EMQX is directly tied to the sensitive data class, so the other agent is cited for the handling path rather than the data class.
conditions: IF regulated IoT data is copied into Plandex-managed files
IF Plandex Cloud or a third-party model provider retains that content beyond policy
mitigations: Keep regulated IoT data out of code workspaces
Use a self-hosted deployment with documented retention
Set explicit deletion procedures for imported artifacts
Separate operational telemetry from development repos
requires-engineering: align retention and residency controls across both systems
